prize_parts.citation: For the theoretical prediction of flat bands in twisted bilayer graphene at a magic angle and the experimental discovery of correlated insulating and superconducting states in this tunable moire system

statement.case_for: Magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene is a discovery in which a clean theoretical prediction (the Bistritzer-MacDonald continuum model, 2011, with vanishing Dirac velocity and flat bands at a magic twist angle) was followed seven years later by an experimental discovery of correlated insulators and unconventional superconductivity at that angle. That theory-experiment loop is what I look for in condensed-matter physics. The platform is tunable by gating and twist angle, it has been reproduced by many groups with several probes (transport, STM, compressibility), and it opened the moire materials field, which now reaches transition-metal dichalcogenides, fractional Chern insulators and beyond. It is also a fresh example of quantum mechanics in materials producing behaviour we did not expect, and the electronic-structure community has been able to test the continuum model against atomistic calculations, so the theory is checkable and not just a story. The attribution can be traced: prediction in 2011, decisive experiment in 2018.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservations are attribution and interpretation. Eva Andrei's group had independent STM evidence of flat-band localization in twisted graphene, and Yuan Cao, first author of the 2018 papers, is outside any three-person list, so any trio leaves out a real claimant. The pairing mechanism of the superconductivity is still debated, and sample-to-sample twist-angle disorder limits reproducibility of the fine details. A committee could reasonably argue that the field has not yet settled on what it has discovered, and that a prize in two or three years would be safer. Against that, the phenomena themselves are robust, which is what the prize would recognise.

responses.point: Lindroth ranks twisted bilayer graphene only sixth because the origin of the superconductivity and sample variability mean the interpretation is not yet stable, and she favours the optical lattice clock and ultracold-atom lattices instead.
responses.response: I take the concern about interpretation seriously, and I would not want a citation that claims an explanation of the superconductivity. But the Nobel Prize has rewarded discoveries of phenomena before their mechanisms were settled, and my proposed citation is worded around the prediction of flat bands and the observation of the correlated and superconducting states, which are independently reproduced. Reproduced phases with an open mechanism is a different situation from an unconfirmed claim. On the clock, I agree that it is a clear and verified advance and I rank it as a credible alternative, but I see it as precision engineering built on the frequency-comb recognition of 2005, whereas twisted graphene opens a new space of quantum phases.

responses.point: Johansson places circuit QED first for opening a new strong-coupling regime of light-matter interaction in a circuit, while noting that the 2025 prize already rewarded superconducting-circuit quantum physics and may make this a repetition.
responses.response: I defer to Johansson on circuit QED, since this is close to his own area, and I agree the discovery of a strong, tunable coupling regime is real. My hesitation is the one he raises himself: after the 2025 macroscopic tunnelling prize, which I chaired, another superconducting-circuit prize looks too close, and a good part of the visible impact is through quantum computing hardware, not a new state of matter. I notice that we agree on twisted bilayer graphene as a strong second choice for him, so I would ask whether he can accept it as a first choice if circuit QED is judged too near the 2025 prize.

responses.point: Danielsson places IceCube first as a clean observational discovery of astrophysical neutrinos, and considers a single laureate (Halzen) defensible, while acknowledging that a large collaboration and earlier pioneers complicate the allocation.
responses.response: Astrophysics is far from my field and I defer to him and Pearce on the discovery itself. My concern is the allocation: a single-name prize for a km3 collaboration with AMANDA predecessors seems to me the thinnest attribution on the shortlist, and Pearce says as much. I would ask whether the committee can identify in the dossier the other decisive figures before this goes forward. I note that Danielsson ranks twisted bilayer graphene second with the same trio I propose, so there is a path to agreement.

responses.point: Mehlig ranks twisted bilayer graphene first for its single simple mechanism (interlayer tunnelling giving flat bands at a magic angle) and a separable prediction and discovery, but concedes that Andrei's earlier work makes a three-person prize contestable.
responses.response: I agree with his reading and with the trio. I would add that the separability he describes is the main reason I prefer prediction plus 2018 experiment over a configuration including Andrei: her STM work showed flat-band localization, but the correlated insulator and superconductivity, which are what made the field, came from the Jarillo-Herrero group. I accept that this is a judgement the committee should make explicitly, and I would be open to hearing whether anyone who has read the 2010-2017 literature more closely sees her contribution as priority for the physics we are citing.

uncertainties: Whether Eva Y. Andrei or Yuan Cao has a claim strong enough to displace one of the three names, and whether early STM flat-band work has priority for any part of the physics
Whether the unsettled pairing mechanism for the superconductivity makes the discovery premature for this year
Whether the topological-insulator branch (B041) should be treated as one decision with the overlapping entries, and who is left out (Mele, Bernevig, Hughes, Zhang, Fu)
Whether circuit QED is too close to the 2025 prize to be seriously considered
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile for B014 or the named alternatives. I chaired the committee for the 2025 prize (macroscopic quantum tunnelling in superconducting circuits), which is relevant to how I weigh B046 but is not a personal connection to any candidate. My collaborators on atomistic spin dynamics and full-potential codes are not on the shortlist.
